request.system:
You review a blog article an online shop is about to publish. You did not write it. You see the shop, the topic and the search it targets, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), and the article. Sentences about products end with the facts they rest on in brackets; [G] marks a sentence the writer says is general knowledge.

Score each from 1 to 5:
- grounding: everything said about the shop's products is exactly what the cited facts say, with nothing added, stretched or implied. One product claim the facts do not support caps this at 2. No invented experience ("we tested", customer stories), statistics or studies.
- information_gain: a shopper who searched this would learn something useful and specific, beyond generic filler they could find anywhere. Padding, repetition and vague praise lower it.
- structure: it answers the search early, its sections follow in a sensible order, headings say what is below them, lists and tables are used where they help.
- fit: it suits this shop, its audience and tone, stays on the topic, and does not read as an advert.
5 is excellent, 4 good enough to publish as it is, 3 acceptable with flaws, 2 or 1 not publishable.

List problems: each with the exact sentence quoted and what is wrong, most serious first. Leave the list empty if there are none.

For each general-knowledge sentence you are given (G1, G2…), answer with its reference and whether every number in it is well established and uncontroversial general knowledge that needs no source (accepted true), or not (false), with a short reason.

<article>
Title: Bike lights for commuting: what to look for before winter

For commuting you need two things from your lights: a front light bright enough to show potholes on unlit stretches, and a rear light that drivers notice from a distance, including in daylight. A front light with a shaped beam, a rear light with a daytime flash mode, and enough battery to last several journeys between charges will cover most commutes.

## Seeing and being seen are different jobs

On lit city streets, the job is to be seen: a steady or pulsing light that makes you obvious to drivers pulling out of junctions. On unlit lanes, canal paths and park routes, the job is to see: a strong, well-shaped beam that shows the surface early enough to react. Many commutes include both, so choose for the darkest part of your route rather than the brightest.

## The front light: brightness and beam shape

Lumens tell you how much light a lamp produces, but where that light goes matters just as much. A round beam throws light into the eyes of oncoming cyclists and drivers, while a shaped beam puts it on the road where you need it.

The [Beacon 800 Front Light](P1) has a maximum output of 800 lumens [F1]. It has a cut-off beam that keeps light below the eye line of oncoming traffic [F4]. The Beacon 800 is rated IPX6 for water resistance [F5].

{{P1}}

## The rear light: visible day and night

Drivers coming up behind you are often looking for cars, not bikes, so a rear light that stands out in daylight as well as at night is worth having. A flashing mode catches the eye better than a steady one in bright conditions.

The [Glow 60 Rear Light](P2) has a maximum output of 60 lumens [F6] and a daytime flash mode [F7]. It mounts on seat posts and seat stays with a rubber strap [F8]. Once it is fitted, check that a saddle bag, a rack or a mudguard is not hiding it.

{{P2}}

## Battery life and charging

Battery life is quoted per mode, and the brightest mode always runs out first. Work out how long your ride is each way, and choose a mode that will last several journeys, not just one.

The Beacon 800 runs for 2 hours on its highest setting and 20 hours on its lowest flashing mode [F2]. It charges by USB-C [F3], so it can be topped up at your desk from a standard USB-C cable. Cold weather shortens battery life generally, so a light that lasted all autumn may need charging more often in the depths of winter.

## Small extras that help

Movement catches a driver's eye. Reflective or fluorescent material at your ankles shows the up-and-down motion of pedalling, which is hard to mistake for anything other than a cyclist. The [Reflective Ankle Bands](P3) are fluorescent yellow [F10] and fasten with hook-and-loop [F9].

{{P3}}

For everything else worth sorting before the dark mornings, see our [winter commuting checklist](L2), or browse all our [bike lights](L1).

</article>
